scenes.tts: Watch one microtubule grow from a seed in a dish of purified tubulin. It lengthens slowly for minutes, then shrinks many times faster than it grew. Sometimes it starts growing again. A crystal in its solution does not behave like this. Why would a polymer be built to fail?
scenes.visual: A short tube of bead rows grows from a grey seed, shrinks fast, regrows; then a question mark.
scenes.narration: Watch one microtubule grow from a seed in a dish of purified tubulin. It lengthens slowly for minutes, then shrinks many times faster than it grew. Sometimes it starts growing again. A crystal in its solution does not behave like this. Why would a polymer be built to fail?

scenes.tts: Plot the length of one plus end against time, in a trace made up for teaching. It grows for three minutes, from five to nine and a half micrometres. That is one and a half micrometres per minute. Then it loses six micrometres in twelve seconds, and the line plunges. That is thirty micrometres per minute, twenty times faster.

scenes.tts: Why does an end fail? Each tubulin dimer joins the end with G T P on its beta-tubulin. The G T P is hydrolysed soon after, once the dimer sits inside the lattice behind the end. G D P tubulin is held in the straight lattice only by its neighbours. The end stays intact while a cap of dimers not yet hydrolysed remains.
scenes.caption: Why does an end fail? Each tubulin dimer joins the end with GTP on its β-tubulin. The GTP is hydrolysed soon after, once the dimer sits inside the lattice behind the end. GDP-tubulin is held in the straight lattice only by its neighbours. The end stays intact while a cap of dimers not yet hydrolysed remains.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the plus end: gold GTP dimers join, columns behind turn blue (GDP), a bracket marks the gold cap.
scenes.narration: Why does an end fail? Each tubulin dimer joins the end with GTP on its β-tubulin. The GTP is hydrolysed soon after, once the dimer sits inside the lattice behind the end. scenes.tts: If addition slows and hydrolysis catches up, the cap is lost. The end comes apart quickly, with protofilaments peeling outward from the tip, and it shortens fast. That switch from growth to shortening is a catastrophe. The switch back is a rescue. Each end switches this way on its own, and the behaviour is called dynamic instability.
scenes.visual: Cap turns blue and rows peel outward; then the full trace returns with catastrophe and rescue marked.

scenes.tts: The cap idea has been tested in experiments. In 2020, a team used recombinant human tubulin carrying mutations that slow hydrolysis. The caps grew longer. Earlier work on pig brain tubulin, free of other proteins, found that more tubulin made catastrophes rarer at both ends. That fits a larger cap at faster growth.

scenes.tts: Binding drives assembly, and hydrolysis comes afterwards and makes the old lattice less stable. A cap of dimers not yet hydrolysed holds the end together. Exactly what commits an end to shortening is still argued. Keep the rule. Lose the cap, and the end shortens rapidly, many times faster than it grew.
